brief_context: Town where the Sparthfield Clinic is located.
article_title: HEALTH • HOPE • HAPPINESS • ELECTRICITY IN THE SPARTHFIELD CLINICS
brief_extract: A. HILL, Magazine Secretary, Rochdale Branch, E.A.W. MOST people on being told they they have to attend a clinic for examination or X-Ray treatment feel apprehension and sometimes real fear.

brief_context: Visible from the grounds of the Sparthfield Clinic.
article_title: HEALTH • HOPE • HAPPINESS • ELECTRICITY IN THE SPARTHFIELD CLINICS
brief_extract: This should not be the case for anyone who is sent to Sparthfield Clinic, Rochdale. Situated in one of the residential areas of the town, it was once a private residence and stands in its own grounds surrounded by trees and well-kept gardens, with a wonderful view of the Lancashire moors. Sparthfield first entered the hospital world in December, 1937, as a Nursing Home founded by Sir Alfred Joseph Law, primarily for the treatment of Parkinson's disease.

brief_context: The name of the clinics being visited and described.
brief_extract: Patients are brought here from as far away as fifty miles and spinal injections are given which relieve the intolerable pain from which they are suffering, pain which in most cases will not respond to any other medical treatment. We concluded our visit with a feeling that Electricity is playing a wonderful part in the medical world today, and it is hoped that Sparthfield Clinics will link even closer the preventative and cura-tive work of the health services of the district. Local authority and hospital staff will continue to work in these premises with the single purpose of preventing ill-ness wherever possible and when-ever it occurs, providing early detection with prompt and effec-tive treatment.

brief_context: The primary subject of the article regarding culinary practices.
brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE JANUARY 1958

EATING IN DENMARK

EATING in Denmark rather bears out the statement that "a little of what you fancy does you good", only in Denmark "a little" becomes "a lot". A Danish meal table, at any time of the day, looks inviting with its colourful assortment of foods which would tickle anyone's fancy, and the sharp, clean flavours of the fish, meat and cheese tickle the palates even of those who profess not to be interested in food.

brief_context: Comparison of Danish food to that of Baltic countries.
brief_extract: Perhaps this is why this drink tastes so much better in its homeland. Danish food, like that of all the Baltic countries, is not so well suited to wine which complements the cuisine of the rest of Europe, but it has a character of its own which is at once interesting and wholesome. It is the cold table which is such a delight in Denmark, and which gives ideas to hostesses in this country arranging a formal cold meal or a buffet function.

brief_context: Mention of Britain's need for skill.
brief_extract: A technical society is at once conferring benefits on women and making greater demands than hitherto. The wide range of automatic equipment in the home, and the use of light-weight, easily washable materials offer emancipation from household drudgery, while Britain’s need of all the skill it can muster is giving women opportunities for satisfying work outside the home. And yet there is a snag; the two lines of opportunity do not meet, for they are deflected by Purchase Tax on electric labour-saving equipment.

brief_context: Location of a lecture on living electrically.
brief_extract:
Meeting country needs

In an age of urbanisation it is refreshing to hear of the advantages which electricity is bringing to remote communities, while their natural amenities are preserved. The Caroline Haslett Trust Lecture on “Living Electrically in North Italy and Austria” illustrates the benefits which are dependent on hydro-electric power. Domestic science training specially adapted to meet the needs of country homes is the subject of an interesting article by the Principal of Radbrook College, Shropshire, and she shows how teachers in the country school must be trained to correlate home-making courses with the work in Rural Science.

brief_context: Location where housecraft teaching was extended in schools.
brief_extract:
Teaching farm skill
Ideas on education developed, the school leaving age was raised and by 1950 the junior course had changed from a mainly vocational training to the equivalent of the last two years of a Secondary Modern education with a strong bias towards home management. As Housecraft teaching in the Shropshire schools was extended, there was no longer a need for this course. Meantime the Sub-Committee for Agricultural Education decided that it was important to provide, end-on to secondary modern schooling, a course for further education for girls who expect to live and work in the county.

Electricity and World Progress
Electricity is becoming one of the symbols of progress in the developing countries in which these women live, and it is only a question of time before it will revolutionise the home life in these territories just as it has in the more advanced countries. Our electrical industry is well aware of the great potentialities for electricity in Africa, Asia and the new West Indian Federation and, in fact, the theme of this year's British Electrical Power Convention at Brighton is "Electricity and World Progress — Britain's Contribution." At the Convention papers will be presented dealing with the development of nuclear energy for electricity supply overseas, Britain's part in electrical development overseas, and British hydro-electric plant and world power requirements. The industry has also seized the opportunity of the great Brussels Exhibition this year to display some of its latest achievements before the eyes of all the world and his wife who will be visiting the exhibition during the next few months.

brief_context: Famous exhibition and festival venue in Glasgow.
brief_extract: The Burgh had the right from the 11th century to hold a weekly market and an annual July Fair. Provand's Lordship is the oldest house in Glasgow, built in 1471, and it was here that Mary Queen of Scots stayed when visiting Lord Darnley in 1566, and where the fatal "casket letters" were probably written.

brief_context: Region where Irish glassware was exported.
article_title: Craft for Beauty and Utility —The History of Waterford Glass
brief_extract: In those days, when the best was always obtainable and taste at its most discriminating, the glass of Waterford graced every household of importance-for the Irish craftsmen not only produced glass of unrivalled brilliance and transparency but also, with truly Irish understanding of human frailties, put rings round the necks of decanters so that they might be more easily grasped by unsteady fingers. A considerable export trade in Irish glassware was built up during this period-mainly to North America and the West Indies. In 1783, George and William Penrose founded the most famous of the Waterford factories; it became the outstanding centre of Irish glass manufacture and earned world fame for its product.

brief_context: Location where the glass industry was revived in 1947.
brief_extract: The onset of the Industrial Revolution brought changes in tempo and taste; the leisured life and refinement of the old era gave way to the drabness and "dark Satanic mills" of the 19th century. The trade in Waterford glass declined and the craft was practically extinguished by 1851. It was revived in 1947 when a small factory was built in Waterford; at present it employs some 500 workers, and works a 16-hour, two-shift day to meet the new demand.

brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE OCTOBER 1958

MISS MARY GEORGE, M.B.E., E.A.W. Director, describes—

EXPO 1958

EXPO 1958, as the Brussels Universal Exhibition is familiarly called,
is undoubtedly the finest shop window of man’s achievements that
there has ever been. It has been made clear from its original
conception that it is not a trade fair in any sense of the term.

brief_context: Represented with pavilions in the Belgian Section.
brief_extract:
THE Exhibition is in four main sections. There is a vast Belgian

brief_context: Comparison of American appliances with their British counterparts.
brief_extract: She was struck by the vast range of consumer goods, especially electrical appliances. The larger American appliances were not very different in principle from their British counterparts, and as far as could be seen, they were well made and well designed, but the batteries of switches, taps and knobs on each washer and cooker were intimidating. It is in the smaller appliances that the imagination has run riot; an electrical appliance seems to be available for every small chore, except perhaps for cleaning the teeth.

brief_context: Site of the experimental Zeta machine.
brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE OCTOBER 1958

BURNING WATER

By PHYLLIS THOMPSON

TO burn water sounds like one of the Labours of Hercules, and one impossible to carry out, but Zeta, the experimental machine at Harwell, is showing us how it can be done. Not only is it a miracle of science, but it is one which will revolutionise our economy.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding water flow calculations for energy production.
brief_extract: The harnessing of thermo-nuclear power will enable an ordinary family living in a small modern house to keep warm for a whole year on the energy derived from a bucket of water, that is, the equivalent of two tons of coal. It has been estimated that the flow of water in the Thames on a summer's day is enough to supply Britain with energy for nearly two years, and a day's flow of river in flood would supply Britain's fuel for a decade. The rain that falls on Britain in an average year would enable the scientists to supply the country with fuel at the present rate of consumption for about 60 million years!

Interesting Events in E.A.W. Branches

VISIT TO BURLINGHAM HORTICULTURAL STATION
By MRS. J.

brief_context: County where the Burlingham Horticultural Station is located.
brief_extract:
V. TAYLOR, Magazine Secretary, Great Yarmouth
Members visited one of the largest horticultural stations in Norfolk, sponsored by the Norfolk Education Authorities. The tomato houses are heated by electricity, and the trusses in large plant pots are well fed by fertiliser, and the plants were about 12 feet high.

brief_context: City where tomatoes from the station are sent to market.
brief_extract: The tomatoes are collected each day and the weight is recorded on a sheet attached to the tomato house. The fruit is sent to a wholesale market in Norwich and dispatched to retailers throughout the Eastern Counties. It was interesting to see young fruit trees which had been grafted and bear- ing fruit the same year.

brief_context: The county where the all-electric farm is located.
brief_extract:
Grass is given great care, and has
constantly been improved since 1933,
in fact, between £10 and £12 an acre
is spent on fertilisers, and it pays
handsomely. The grass, cut by harvesters, is
taken under cover to the grass drying
plant, which has been used for the
past 12 years and is the only one in
Sussex. Within 20 minutes of the
grass being fed into the machine it
emerges either as hay or meal cubes
—so they really make hay on rainy
days!
